questions.question: How do switch expressions differ from switch statements in Java? Cover arrow syntax, `yield`, exhaustiveness, and the path to pattern matching.
questions.title: Switch Expressions in Java — Arrow Syntax, `yield`, Exhaustiveness
questions.direct_answer: **Switch expressions** (Java 14, JEP 361) make `switch` produce a value, eliminate **fall-through bugs**, and require **exhaustive coverage**. The new **arrow syntax** — `case A -> result` — evaluates one branch and returns a value; **no `break` required**. **Multiple labels per case**: `case MONDAY, TUESDAY, WEDNESDAY -> "Weekday"` replaces the old fall-through pattern. For multi-statement blocks, use **`yield`** to return a value from the block: `case X -> { ... yield value; }`. Switch expressions must be **exhaustive** — the compiler verifies all possible inputs are covered (no unhandled case, or a `default`). For **enums**, listing every constant satisfies exhaustiveness without `default`; for sealed types (Java 17+), listing every permitted subtype does the same. **Old switch statements still work** unchanged for backward compatibility, and you can use the arrow syntax in statements too. The deeper win is conceptual: switch becomes a **first-class expression** that can be used in `return`, in field initializers, and in method arguments — not just a control structure. This is the foundation that **Java 21 pattern matching for switch (JEP 441)** builds on, adding type patterns, record deconstruction, and `when` guards. Together they push Java toward algebraic-data-type-style matching seen in Scala and Kotlin.

sections.content:
**Always prefer switch expression over statement** when you want a value:
- Cleaner.
- Exhaustive (compiler-checked).
- Eliminates `default` for enums/sealed types.
- One-liner for many cases.

**Use arrow syntax everywhere**:
- No fall-through.
- No `break`.
- Multi-label is comma-separated.

**Use `yield` only when you need a block** — for single-expression cases, the arrow alone is enough.

**Don't use `default` for enum/sealed switches**:
- Defeats the exhaustiveness check.
- New enum constants won't trigger compile errors.
- Use `default -> throw new IllegalStateException(...)` only as a defensive 'should never happen' marker.

**Migration**:
- IDEs (IntelliJ, Eclipse) auto-convert old switch to switch expression.
- Usually safe; verify behavior on edge cases (especially fall-through).
- Remove `default` clauses for enum switches once converted.

**Style**:
- Align arrow `->` for readability if many cases.
- Group related labels with comma: `case A, B, C -> ...`
- For complex per-case logic, extract to methods rather than blocks: `case X -> handleX(args);`

**Pitfalls**:
- **Mixing arrow and colon**: compile error. Pick one.
- **`yield` vs `return`**: `yield` exits the case block; `return` exits the method.
- **Statement vs expression**: only expressions enforce exhaustiveness; statements don't.
- **Enum/sealed without `default`**: works, but adding new constants forces updates everywhere (this is usually what you want).
- **Java 14–16 versions** — the feature was preview in 12–13, finalized in 14. Use Java 17 LTS or later for production.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Switch expressions** (Java 14, JEP 361) fix the long-standing problems with Java's `switch` statement.

**Three big improvements**

**1. Arrow syntax**
- `case A -> result` — no `break`, no fall-through
- Multiple labels: `case A, B, C -> result`
- Each case is independent

**2. Returns a value**
- Switch becomes an expression — usable in `return`, field initializers, method args
- No need to declare a variable outside and mutate inside

**3. Exhaustive**
- Compiler verifies all cases covered
- Adding a new enum constant or sealed subtype → compile error in every switch
- Massive maintenance win

**`yield` for multi-statement cases**
- Use a block when you need multiple statements
- `yield` returns the value from the block to the switch expression
- `case X -> { log.info(...); yield value; }`
- `yield` vs `return` — yield exits the case block; return exits the method

**Exhaustiveness rules**

**For enums** — listing all constants is exhaustive
- No `default` needed
- Adding a new constant → compile error in every switch
- This is the biggest win for evolving codebases

**For sealed types (Java 17+)** — listing all permitted subtypes is exhaustive
- No `default` needed
- Foundation for ADT-style matching

**For other types** (int, String, etc.) — must include `default`
- Compiler can't enumerate all values

**Arrow in statements too**
- `switch (event) { case CLICK -> handleClick(event); ... }` — no return value
- Still no fall-through, still no break
- Useful for side-effect-only dispatch

**Forbidden mixing**
- Cannot mix arrow and colon cases in one switch
- Compile error
- Pick one style per switch

**Switch statement vs expression — which to use**

**Switch expression** — when you want a value
- Exhaustive (compiler-checked)
- Cleaner
- One-liner for many cases

**Switch statement (arrow)** — side effects only
- No value, but still safe (no fall-through)
- For event dispatch, etc.

**Switch statement (colon + break)** — legacy or fall-through needed
- Rare; usually a smell
- Old code; not for new

**Java 21 pattern matching — the deeper payoff**

**Type patterns**
- `case Integer i -> ...` — binds `i` to the matched type
- `case String s -> ...`
- `case null -> ...` — null is its own case

**Record deconstruction (JEP 440)**
- `case Point(int x, int y) -> ...` — destructure inline
- Nested: `case Line(Point(int x1, int y1), Point(int x2, int y2)) -> ...`

**`when` guards**
- `case Integer i when i > 100 -> "large"`
- Add a predicate to a type pattern

**Sealed types + pattern switch = ADT matching**
- Compiler verifies exhaustiveness over the closed hierarchy
- No `default` needed
- Same expressive power as Scala/Kotlin sealed match

**Migration tips**
- IDEs auto-convert old switch — generally safe
- Verify edge cases (especially intentional fall-through, which is rare)
- Remove `default` from enum/sealed switches — keep exhaustiveness check
- Use `default -> throw new IllegalStateException(...)` only as a defensive marker for impossible cases

**Best practices**
- Always prefer expression over statement when value is needed
- Use arrow everywhere — avoid colon
- `yield` only when you need a block
- Don't add `default` to enum/sealed switches
- Group related labels with commas
- Extract complex case logic to methods

**Recommendation:** Use **switch expressions with arrow syntax** as your default for any 'compute a value based on a discriminator' pattern. They eliminate fall-through bugs, force exhaustiveness, and make the intent ("this is computing a result") obvious. For **enum** discriminators, leave off `default` so the compiler will alert you when new constants are added — this is the most powerful maintenance feature. For **sealed types** (Java 17+), do the same; combined with **pattern matching for switch** in Java 21, you get full ADT-style matching with compile-time exhaustiveness, putting Java on par with Scala and Kotlin for type-driven dispatch. Use **`yield`** only when a case needs multiple statements; otherwise the arrow alone is cleanest. **Never mix arrow and colon** styles in the same switch — compile error. **Trust your IDE** to convert legacy switch statements; it's usually a safe refactor that improves clarity. The deeper lesson: switch is no longer just a control structure — it's a first-class expression and the gateway to Java's modern pattern-matching family.

questions.question: What is pattern matching for `instanceof` in Java? How does it improve downcasting?
questions.title: Pattern Matching for `instanceof` — Cleaner Downcasting (Java 16+)
questions.direct_answer: **Pattern matching for `instanceof`** (Java 16, JEP 394, preview in 14–15) lets you **declare and bind a pattern variable in the `instanceof` check itself** — eliminating the redundant cast that was required for decades. Instead of `if (obj instanceof String) { String s = (String) obj; ... }`, you write `if (obj instanceof String s) { ... }` and `s` is automatically bound to `obj` as a `String`. The pattern variable is **scoped only where the check proves true** — it's in scope inside the `if` block's true branch, in the right side of `&&` expressions, and (via clever flow analysis) in `else` branches where the type has been eliminated. The compiler also **rejects redundant patterns** — `if (x instanceof String s) { ... } else if (x instanceof String t) { ... }` doesn't compile because `t` can never bind. Beyond the syntax win, pattern matching is the foundation for **switch pattern matching** (Java 21, JEP 441) and **record deconstruction patterns** (Java 21). The cognitive model shifts from "check then cast" to "match and bind" — safer, shorter, and aligned with functional languages like Scala and Kotlin. Combined with sealed classes (Java 17), you get exhaustive type matching with compiler verification.

sections.content:
**Use `instanceof` pattern matching**:
- Everywhere you previously wrote `if (x instanceof T) { T t = (T) x; ... }` — it's strictly better.
- In `equals` implementations — one of the cleanest wins.
- Combined with early-return negation for clean guard clauses.
- For simple type dispatch (2–3 types).

**Prefer switch pattern matching (Java 21)** when:
- Dispatching on many types.
- Working with sealed hierarchies.
- Needing exhaustiveness checking.

**Caveats**:
- **Generic types**: `if (x instanceof List<String>)` doesn't work due to erasure; use `List<?>` and cast inside or trust your data.
- **Primitive types**: can't pattern-match primitives directly — `int` requires `Integer`.
- **Subclasses and interface hierarchies**: the compiler rejects unreachable patterns, which sometimes requires reordering.
- **Scope subtleties**: flow scoping is powerful but can surprise.

**Style**:
- Name pattern variables meaningfully — not `s`, `t`, `x`. Use `user`, `order`, `event`.
- Keep patterns simple — if a chain of `instanceof` + `&&` gets long, switch to pattern switch.

**Performance**:
- Identical bytecode to the old form.
- No runtime overhead.
- Purely a source-level improvement.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pattern matching for `instanceof`** (Java 16, JEP 394) introduces pattern variables in the check itself.
- **Syntax**: `if (obj instanceof Type var) { /* var in scope */ }`.
- **Flow scoping**: pattern variable in scope wherever the compiler can prove the check succeeded.
- **Works in `&&` chains**: `obj instanceof String s && s.length() > 5`.
- **Works with negation + early exit**: `if (!(obj instanceof User u)) return;` then `u` is in scope below.
- **Does NOT work in `||` chains** — the variable might not be bound.
- **Compiler rejects redundant/unreachable patterns**.
- **Generic types** require wildcards: `instanceof List<?>`, not `instanceof List<String>`.
- **No primitive pattern matching** yet (boxed types only).
- **Foundation for switch pattern matching** (Java 21, JEP 441) and **record deconstruction** (JEP 440).
- **Exhaustive switch + sealed classes** (Java 21) gives ADT-style type matching with compile-time checks.
- **Same bytecode** as old `instanceof` + cast — zero runtime cost.
- **IDEs auto-suggest** the conversion; always safe to accept.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Pattern matching for `instanceof` (Java 16, JEP 394) lets you declare and bind a pattern variable in the `instanceof` check itself — eliminating the redundant cast that Java required for decades.

**Before Java 16**
- `if (obj instanceof String) { String s = (String) obj; ... }`
- Redundant: compiler just proved it's a String, but the type system didn't carry that

**Java 16+**
- `if (obj instanceof String s) { ... }`
- `s` is a **pattern variable** — declared and bound in the same expression
- No cast, no duplicate type name, no risk of typo

**Flow scoping — where the pattern variable lives**

The variable is in scope wherever the compiler can prove the check succeeded.

**In the true branch**: always in scope

**With `&&`**: extends scope to the RHS
- `obj instanceof String s && s.length() > 5` — `s` usable on the right side

**With `||`**: does NOT extend scope
- `obj instanceof String s || s.length() > 5` — compile error on `s`

**With negation + early return/throw**:
- `if (!(obj instanceof User u)) return;`
- `process(u);` — u in scope here
- The compiler tracks: if we didn't return, `u` must be bound

**NOT in the else branch** after a positive match

**Compiler rejects redundant patterns**
- Same-type re-check in else — error
- Unreachable subtype after supertype — error
- Already-bound variable shadow — error

**Practical wins**
- Cleaner `equals`
- Early-return guards: `if (!(entity instanceof Order order)) return BigDecimal.ZERO;`
- Type dispatch in event handlers (use switch pattern for many)
- Nested with `&&`

**Caveats**
- Generic types: `instanceof List<?>` only — erasure prevents `List<String>`
- Primitives: can't pattern-match `int`; use `Integer`
- Scope subtleties: flow scoping is powerful but worth understanding

**Foundation for later JEPs**

**Switch pattern matching (Java 21, JEP 441)** — same binding in switch cases

**Record deconstruction (Java 21, JEP 440)** — destructure inline

**Guards with `when` (Java 21)** — add a predicate to a type pattern

**Sealed types + switch patterns = exhaustive matching**

**Performance**
- Zero runtime cost
- Same bytecode as old `instanceof` + cast
- Purely a source-level improvement

**Recommendation:** Use pattern matching for `instanceof` **everywhere** you previously wrote `instanceof` + cast — it's strictly better, same bytecode, zero risk. Your IDE will suggest the conversion automatically. Lean on **flow scoping**: combine with negation and early-return for clean guard clauses (`if (!(x instanceof User u)) return; process(u);`). For dispatching on many types, graduate to **switch pattern matching** (Java 21) — especially with **sealed classes**, where the compiler enforces exhaustiveness. Remember the generic-types caveat: you can't write `instanceof List<String>` due to erasure; use `List<?>` and narrow inside. Name pattern variables **meaningfully** (`user`, `order`, `event`), not single letters. This feature is the gateway to the full Java 21 pattern-matching family: `switch` patterns, record deconstruction, guards with `when` — all designed to make Java feel more like Scala/Kotlin without sacrificing type safety.

questions.question: What are Java text blocks and how do incidental whitespace and escape rules work?
questions.title: Text Blocks in Java — Multi-Line Strings, Incidental Whitespace, Escape Tricks
questions.direct_answer: **Text blocks** (Java 15, JEP 378, preview in 13–14) are **multi-line string literals** delimited by triple quotes (`"""`). They eliminate the noise of `\n` and `+` concatenation when embedding SQL, JSON, HTML, or any multi-line text in Java. The defining feature is **incidental whitespace stripping**: the compiler determines a common indentation prefix — usually the indentation of the **closing `"""`** — and removes that many leading spaces from every line. So your text block visually aligns with surrounding Java code, but the resulting string has no leading indentation. The opening `"""` must be followed by a line terminator (you can't put text on the opening line). Inside, **double quotes don't need escaping** (only `"""` itself does, and only if it appears literally), and **backslash escapes still work**. Two special escapes are unique to text blocks: **`\<newline>`** (line continuation — join the next line without a newline) and **`\s`** (literal space, useful to preserve trailing whitespace which would otherwise be stripped). You can also use **`String.formatted(args...)`** (Java 15) as a fluent inline alternative to `String.format` — great for templating values into a text block. Text blocks are **not interpolated** (Java's string templates JEP was withdrawn); to inject values you use `formatted` or string concatenation. The win: SQL queries, JSON payloads, HTML snippets, and GraphQL queries become readable as their natural form. The major use case in real codebases is `@Query` annotations in Spring Data and JSON test fixtures.

sections.title: The Problem Text Blocks Solve
sections.content:
Embedding multi-line text in Java was always painful:

```java
String sql = "SELECT u.id, u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count\n" +
             "FROM users u\n" +
             "LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id\n" +
             "WHERE u.active = true\n" +
             "GROUP BY u.id, u.name\n" +
             "HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 0";
```

**Issues**:
- Visual noise: `\n`, `"+"`, redundant quoting.
- Hard to copy from a SQL editor.
- No indentation that matches both Java context and SQL natural form.
- Easy to break alignment when editing.

With text blocks (Java 15, JEP 378):
```java
String sql = """
        SELECT u.id, u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
        FROM users u
        LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
        WHERE u.active = true
        GROUP BY u.id, u.name
        HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 0
        """;
```

Readable as SQL. Indentation matches the Java context. The compiler strips the leading 8 spaces from each line (because the closing `"""` is at column 8).

sections.title: Syntax Rules
sections.content:
**Opening delimiter**:
- `"""` followed by **a line terminator** (newline) — nothing else allowed on the same line.
- This is a compile error: `String s = """ hello """;`

**Closing delimiter**:
- `"""` on its own line OR at the end of a line.
- Position determines indentation stripping.

**Content**:
- Each line up to the closing `"""` is part of the string.
- Newlines in source become `\n` in the result (always LF, regardless of platform).

**Quoting inside**:
- Single `"` or `""` are literal — no escape needed.
- `"""` must be escaped as `\"""` (only the conflict with the delimiter).

**Examples**:
```java
String poem = """
        Roses are red,
        Violets are blue,
        Text blocks are great
        And so are you.
        """;

String json = """
        {
          "name": "Alice",
          "role": "admin"
        }
        """;
// Note: double quotes inside don't need escaping

String withTriple = """
        She said \"""hello\""" loudly.
        """;
// Only literal """ needs escaping
```

sections.title: Incidental Whitespace — The Crucial Rule
sections.content:
The compiler determines a **common minimum indentation prefix** across all lines (including a blank line containing the closing `"""`) and strips it.

**Algorithm**:
1. Look at every line in the text block, including the line with the closing `"""`.
2. For non-blank lines, count the leading whitespace.
3. Take the **minimum** of all those counts (and of the closing delimiter's indent).
4. Strip that many leading spaces from every line.

**Example — closing `"""` controls the strip**:
```java
String result = """
        Hello
        World
        """;
// All lines have 8 leading spaces; closing """ at column 8.
// Min indentation = 8. Result: "Hello\nWorld\n"
```

**Closing `"""` indented less → lines keep more indent**:
```java
String result = """
        Hello
        World
""";
// Lines have 8 spaces; closing """ at column 0.
// Min indentation = 0. Result: "        Hello\n        World\n"
```

**Closing `"""` on the same line as last content**:
```java
String s = """
        Hello
        World""";
// Last line has no newline before """; result has no trailing newline.
// Indentation strip: 8 spaces. Result: "Hello\nWorld"
```

**Mixed indentation — takes the minimum**:
```java
String s = """
        Hello
      World
        """;
// Line 1: 8 spaces, Line 2: 6 spaces, closing: 8 spaces.
// Min = 6. Result: "  Hello\nWorld\n"
// (Line 1 keeps the extra 2 spaces relative to the strip)
```

**Trailing whitespace** on each line is automatically **stripped** unless escaped (see `\s` below).

**Best practice**:
- Place the closing `"""` at the indentation level you want stripped (usually aligned with the surrounding Java code).
- Indent content lines further if you want them indented in the result.

sections.title: Escape Tricks Unique to Text Blocks
sections.content:
**`\<newline>` — line continuation** (join the next line without a newline):
```java
String line = """
        This is one logical line \
        even though it spans two lines in source.
        """;
// Result: "This is one logical line even though it spans two lines in source.\n"
```
Useful for very long URLs or SQL clauses where you want source-level wrapping but a single line of output.

**`\s` — preserve trailing whitespace** (which is otherwise stripped per line):
```java
String table = """
        red  \s
        blue \s
        green\s
        """;
// Each line keeps its trailing spaces; result lines have consistent length.
// Without \s, trailing spaces would be removed.
```

**Standard escapes still work**:
- `\n` — newline (rarely needed; just press Enter).
- `\t` — tab.
- `\\` — backslash.
- `\"` — double quote (not needed inside text block unless followed by more `"`).
- `\u00XX` — unicode escapes work (but they're processed before the parser sees the text block, like in regular strings).

**Combined**:
```java
String config = """
        # Database settings (note: trailing spaces preserved)
        url=jdbc:postgres://localhost:5432/mydb\s
        user=admin\s
        # Long URL on one logical line
        callbackUrl=https://example.com/very/long/path/that/we/want/\
        broken/across/lines/in/source/only
        """;
```

sections.title: Interpolating Values — `formatted` and Friends
Real-World Examples
Useful String API Additions (Java 11–15)
sections.content:
Text blocks come with a family of useful `String` methods added in nearby releases:

**`isBlank()`** (Java 11) — true for empty or whitespace-only:
```java
"".isBlank();        // true
"  ".isBlank();       // true
"\t\n".isBlank();    // true
"a".isBlank();        // false
```

**`strip()`, `stripLeading()`, `stripTrailing()`** (Java 11) — Unicode-aware trim:
```java
"  hello  ".strip();         // "hello"
"  hello  ".stripLeading();  // "hello  "
"  hello  ".stripTrailing(); // "  hello"
// Better than trim() for Unicode whitespace
```

**`repeat(int)`** (Java 11):
```java
"ab".repeat(3);    // "ababab"
"-".repeat(80);    // 80 dashes
```

**`lines()`** (Java 11) — stream over lines:
```java
long count = multiLineText.lines().count();
List<String> nonEmpty = textBlock.lines()
    .filter(line -> !line.isBlank())
    .toList();
```

**`formatted(args)`** (Java 15) — fluent format:
```java
"Name: %s, age: %d".formatted(name, age);
```

**`stripIndent()`** and **`translateEscapes()`** (Java 15) — lower-level methods used internally by text blocks; exposed for runtime processing of strings that look like text blocks (loaded from files, etc.).

**`indent(int)`** (Java 12) — add or remove leading spaces:
```java
"hello".indent(4);    // "    hello\n"
"  hello".indent(-2); // "hello\n"
```

sections.title: Best Practices and Gotchas
sections.content:
**Use text blocks for**:
- SQL queries (especially `@Query` annotations).
- JSON / XML / GraphQL test fixtures and payloads.
- HTML snippets in templates.
- Multi-line error messages.
- Embedded scripts (Bash, JavaScript) in code.

**Don't use text blocks for**:
- Single-line strings — use regular literals.
- User-facing UI text — use ResourceBundle or i18n libraries.
- Anything where templates / interpolation libraries are appropriate (Thymeleaf, FreeMarker, Mustache).

**Best practices**:
- **Place closing `"""`** at the same indentation as you want stripped (typically aligning with surrounding Java).
- **Indent content** further than the closing `"""` to add per-line indentation.
- **Use `\s`** if you need trailing whitespace preserved (rare).
- **Use `\<newline>`** for line continuation within a single logical line.
- **Use `formatted`** for value injection — cleaner than concatenation.
- **Don't fight the indentation** — if your text block looks weirdly aligned, the closing `"""` is in the wrong place.

**Common gotchas**:

**1. Text on the opening line — compile error**:
```java
String s = """ hello """;  // ERROR: opening must be followed by newline
```

**2. Trailing whitespace silently stripped**:
```java
String s = """
        hello   
        world
        """;
// The 3 trailing spaces after 'hello' are GONE
// Use \s if you need them
```

**3. Indentation drift after editing**:
- IDEs sometimes reformat text blocks; review changes carefully.
- Use `// @formatter:off` if necessary.

**4. Line endings**:
- Result always uses `\n` (LF), regardless of source file line endings.
- For Windows line endings in output, use `formatted` or replace explicitly.

**5. No interpolation**:
- `"""\nName: ${name}\n"""` is **literal** — no expansion.
- String templates JEP was withdrawn; use `.formatted(...)`.

**6. Performance**:
- Compile-time concatenation — same as old `"+"` joins after JIT.
- `formatted` is `String.format` underneath — mild overhead vs concatenation but usually negligible.

**Migration from old multi-line strings**:
- IntelliJ/Eclipse offer auto-conversion.
- Generally safe; review for whitespace differences.
- Watch for trailing whitespace that was intentional in the old version.

sections.content:
- **Text blocks** (Java 15, JEP 378) are multi-line string literals delimited by `"""`.
- **Opening `"""` must be followed by a newline** — no text on the same line.
- **Incidental whitespace stripping**: compiler removes the common minimum indent from all lines.
- **Closing `"""` position** controls how much leading whitespace is stripped.
- **Trailing whitespace per line is stripped** unless escaped with `\s`.
- **`\<newline>`** — line continuation; joins next line without a newline in result.
- **`\s`** — literal space; preserves trailing whitespace.
- **Double quotes inside don't need escaping** unless they form `"""`.
- **Result always uses LF (`\n`)** regardless of source file line endings.
- **No string interpolation** — use **`formatted(args)`** (Java 15) for value injection.
- **String templates JEP withdrawn** — not coming in current form.
- **`String.formatted`** (Java 15) is the fluent equivalent of `String.format`.
- **Companion methods**: `isBlank`, `strip`, `repeat`, `lines`, `indent`, `stripIndent`, `translateEscapes`.
- **Best uses**: SQL queries, JSON fixtures, HTML snippets, GraphQL queries, multi-line error messages.
- **IDEs auto-convert** old multi-line concats; review for trailing whitespace.
- **Same bytecode** as old concatenation (compile-time constant folding for static blocks).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Text blocks (Java 15, JEP 378) are multi-line string literals delimited by triple quotes (`"""`). They eliminate the noise of `\n` and `+` concatenation when embedding SQL, JSON, HTML, or any multi-line text.

**Syntax basics**
- Opening `"""` must be followed by a newline — no text on the same line
- Closing `"""` on its own line OR at end of last line
- Position of closing `"""` determines indentation stripping

**Incidental whitespace stripping — the crucial rule**
- Compiler finds the common minimum leading-whitespace prefix across all lines
- Strips that many leading spaces from each line
- Closing `"""` indentation participates in the calculation
- Result: text aligns visually with Java code, but has no extra leading indent in the string

**Quoting inside**
- Single `"` doesn't need escaping
- Only `"""` itself needs escaping (rare)

**Two unique escapes**

**`\<newline>` — line continuation**
- Joins next line without a newline in the result
- Useful for very long URLs or single-line SQL clauses you want wrapped in source

**`\s` — literal space, preserves trailing whitespace**
- Per-line trailing whitespace is auto-stripped
- `\s` opts back in: `"red   \s"` keeps the spaces

**Standard escapes still work**: `\n`, `\t`, `\\`, `\u00XX`

**Result always uses LF (`\n`)**
- Regardless of source file line endings
- For Windows endings in output, use `formatted` or replace explicitly

**No string interpolation — use `formatted`**
- `${...}` is literal in text blocks — no expansion
- String templates JEP was withdrawn (design concerns)
- Use **`String.formatted(args...)`** (Java 15) — fluent inline alternative to `String.format`
- Same format spec; reads naturally chained off the text block
- For complex templating, use Mustache/FreeMarker/Pebble — not text blocks + concat

**Companion String methods (Java 11–15)**
- `isBlank()` — empty or whitespace-only
- `strip()`, `stripLeading()`, `stripTrailing()` — Unicode-aware trim
- `repeat(n)` — repeat the string n times
- `lines()` — stream of lines
- `indent(n)` — add/remove leading spaces
- `stripIndent()`, `translateEscapes()` — lower-level for runtime text-block processing
- `formatted(args)` — fluent format

**Best uses**
- SQL queries (especially `@Query` annotations in Spring Data)
- JSON / XML / GraphQL test fixtures
- HTML snippets in templates
- Multi-line error messages
- Embedded scripts (Bash, JavaScript) in code

**Don't use for**
- Single-line strings — use regular literals
- User-facing UI text — use ResourceBundle or i18n libraries
- Anything where dedicated templating libraries fit better

**Common gotchas**

**1. Text on opening line** — compile error
- `""" hello """` — doesn't compile

**2. Trailing whitespace silently stripped**
- 'hello   \n' becomes 'hello\n'
- Use `\s` if you need them preserved

**3. Indentation drift after IDE reformatting**
- Review autoformatter changes
- Use `// @formatter:off` if necessary

**4. Line endings always LF**
- For Windows line endings in output, replace or format explicitly

**5. No interpolation**
- Use `.formatted(args)` for value injection

**Performance**
- Compile-time concatenation — same bytecode as old `+` joins
- `formatted` mild overhead vs raw concat — usually negligible

**Recommendation:** Use **text blocks** as your default for any **multi-line string** — SQL queries, JSON payloads, HTML snippets, GraphQL queries, multi-line error messages. The most common real-world use is **`@Query`** annotations in Spring Data and **JSON test fixtures**. Place the **closing `"""`** at the same indentation as your surrounding Java (usually 8 spaces in for a method body) — this controls the strip and gives you visual alignment with code without leading indent in the string. Remember: **trailing whitespace per line is auto-stripped** — use **`\s`** if you need it preserved (rare). Use **`\<newline>`** for line continuation when a long logical line needs source-level wrapping. For value injection, use **`String.formatted(args...)`** (Java 15) — it's a fluent alternative to `String.format` that chains naturally off the text block. **Java does NOT have string interpolation** — the templates JEP was withdrawn over safety/design concerns; don't expect `${name}` to work. Pair text blocks with the **String API additions** (`isBlank`, `strip`, `lines`, `repeat`, `indent`) for complete multi-line text handling. The mental model: text blocks are like Heredoc in Bash or triple-quoted strings in Python — same idea, with Java's incidental-whitespace twist for clean alignment with surrounding code.

questions.question: What are Java Records? Cover when to use them, compact constructors, and their limitations vs traditional classes/Lombok.
questions.title: Java Records (Java 16+) — Concise Immutable Data Carriers
questions.direct_answer: **Records** (Java 16, JEP 395) are a concise way to declare **immutable data carrier classes**. One line: `record User(Long id, String name, String email) {}` and the compiler generates: a **canonical constructor** taking all fields, **public accessor methods** named after each field (`id()`, `name()`, `email()` — not `getId()`), `equals` and `hashCode` based on all fields, and a `toString` showing all fields. Records are **implicitly final**, **all fields are final**, and they **implicitly extend `java.lang.Record`** (so they can't extend any other class — but they can implement interfaces). For validation or normalization, use a **compact constructor** — `public Money { Objects.requireNonNull(amount); ... }` — which runs after the parameters are set, before assignment. You can add **static factories**, **custom methods**, **nested records**, and even **a non-canonical constructor** that delegates to the canonical one. Best uses: **DTOs** (request/response models), **value objects** (Money, Coordinate, DateRange), **domain events**, **method return types** for grouping multiple values. Limitations: **not for JPA `@Entity`** (JPA needs a no-arg constructor and mutable state — records have neither), **not for objects with identity** (use a class), **no inheritance** (compose instead). Compared to **Lombok** `@Value`/`@Data`: records are part of the JDK (no annotation processor), are recognized natively by tools, deconstruct in switch patterns (Java 21), and require less compile-time magic. Records also pair perfectly with **sealed types** (Java 17) for ADT-style modeling — `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square` with each subtype as a record.

sections.title: What Records Replace
What the Compiler Generates
Compact Constructor — Validation and Normalization
Adding Methods, Static Factories, Interfaces
Records + Sealed Types = ADTs
Records with Jackson, Spring, and Tools
When NOT to Use Records
sections.content:
**Don't use records for**:

**1. JPA Entities**
- JPA requires no-arg constructor (records require all-args).
- JPA assumes mutable fields with setters.
- Records can't be `@Entity`. Use a class for entities; map to records as DTOs.

**2. Objects with identity (not value semantics)**
- A `User` with a database ID is identified by ID, not by all fields.
- Records auto-generate equals based on all fields — wrong for identity-based.
- Use a class with explicit `equals`/`hashCode` based on ID.

**3. Mutable state**
- Records have only final fields — by design.
- Need a mutable counter, builder, or stateful object? Use a class.
- Workaround: 'wither' methods like `withName(String n)` that return a new record.

**4. Complex inheritance hierarchies**
- Records can implement interfaces but not extend classes.
- For shared implementation, use composition: a delegate class as a field.

**5. Cases where Lombok's flexibility is needed**
- `@Builder`, `@Data` with mutable setters, `@Slf4j` logger generation — records don't replace these.
- For pure immutable data carriers, records win. For other Lombok features, mix as needed.

**6. Internal mutable buffers / large arrays**
- Records by reference — copying a 1M-element array record involves the array reference, not deep copy. The array itself is mutable.
- For genuinely immutable collections, use `List.copyOf` in the compact constructor:
```java
public record Configuration(List<String> tags) {
    public Configuration {
        tags = List.copyOf(tags);  // defensive immutable copy
    }
}
```

**7. Records with fewer than ~3 components are sometimes overkill**
- A `record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second)` is cute but `Map.Entry` exists.
- Don't ship a record for two ints if a method-local class would do.

**Style recommendations**:
- **Use records for DTOs, value objects, return-grouping types, domain events**.
- **Use classes for entities, services, mutable state, identity-based objects**.
- **Prefer records over Lombok `@Value`** for new code (portability, tooling, deconstruction).
- **Don't add too many custom methods** — records are data carriers; if you need behavior, consider whether a class is more appropriate.
- **Use compact constructors for validation** — fail fast on invalid input.

sections.content:

- **Auto-generated**: canonical constructor, accessors (named after fields, not `get*`), `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`.
- **Implicitly `final`** and **implicitly extends `Record`** — cannot extend other classes.
- **Can implement interfaces** and contain custom methods, static factories, nested types.
- **Compact constructor** for validation/normalization: `public Money { ... }` — no parameter list, no field assignments (implicit).
- **Non-canonical constructors must delegate** to the canonical via `this(...)`.
- **No instance fields** beyond components; static fields/methods OK.
- **Accessors are `name()`, `id()`** — NOT `getName()`. JavaBean-style getters not generated.
- **Component-wise equals/hashCode/toString** — value semantics.
- **Pair perfectly with sealed types** (Java 17) for ADT-style modeling.
- **Deconstruct in switch patterns** (Java 21) — `case Circle(double r) -> ...`.
- **Don't use for**: JPA entities, identity-based objects, mutable state, complex inheritance.
- **Defensive copies** — use `List.copyOf` in compact constructor for collection components.
- **Jackson 2.12+** recognizes records natively; **Bean Validation 3.0+** validates record components.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Records (Java 16, JEP 395) are a concise way to declare immutable data carrier classes. One line: `record User(Long id, String name, String email) {}` and the compiler generates everything.

**What the compiler generates**
- Canonical constructor taking all fields
- Public accessor methods named after each field — `id()`, `name()` (NOT `getId()`)
- `equals` and `hashCode` based on all components
- `toString` showing all fields

**Implicit rules**
- Records are `final` — can't be subclassed
- Records implicitly extend `java.lang.Record` — can't extend other classes
- Can implement interfaces
- All fields are `private final`

**Compact constructor for validation/normalization**
- `public Money { Objects.requireNonNull(amount); currency = currency.toUpperCase(); }`
- No parameter list — they're already in scope
- No `this.x = x` — assignment is automatic after the body
- Reassigning the parameter normalizes the value (field gets the new value)
- Throw to fail validation

**You can add**
- Custom methods
- Static factories
- Nested records
- Static fields/methods
- Non-canonical constructors (must delegate via `this(...)`)

**You CANNOT add**
- Instance fields beyond components
- Mutable state
- Inheritance from other classes

**Records pair perfectly with sealed types (Java 17) — ADTs**
- `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square` with each subtype as a record
- Pattern matching switch (Java 21) deconstructs them
- `case Circle(double r) -> Math.PI * r * r`
- Compiler verifies exhaustiveness
- Same expressive power as Scala case classes or Rust enums

**Best uses**
- DTOs (request/response models)
- Value objects (Money, Coordinate, DateRange)
- Domain events
- Method return types for grouping multiple values
- Pattern matching with sealed types

**When NOT to use records**

**1. JPA `@Entity`**
- JPA needs no-arg constructor and mutable fields
- Records have neither
- Use a class for entities; map to records as DTOs

**2. Identity-based objects**
- A `User` identified by ID, not all fields
- Records auto-generate equals based on all fields — wrong
- Use a class with explicit equals based on ID

**3. Mutable state**
- Records have only final fields
- For mutable: use a class
- 'Wither' workaround: `withName(String n)` returns a new record

**4. Complex inheritance**
- Can implement interfaces, can't extend classes
- For shared implementation: composition

**5. Defensive copies for mutable components**
- Records hold references; List/Map components are still mutable through the reference
- Use `List.copyOf(tags)` in compact constructor for true immutability

**Records vs Lombok `@Value`**
- Records: native JDK, no annotation processor, work in IDEs without plugins
- Records: recognized by Jackson, Spring, Bean Validation natively
- Records: deconstruct in pattern matching switch (Java 21)
- Lombok still useful for `@Builder`, mutable `@Data`, `@Slf4j` — records don't replace those
- For new code: prefer records for pure immutable data

**Records with Jackson**
- Jackson 2.12+ recognizes records natively
- Deserializes via canonical constructor
- Field name matches JSON property by default

**Records with Bean Validation**
- Annotate components: `record CreateRequest(@NotBlank String name, @Email String email) {}`
- Works with Jakarta Validation 3.0+

**Records with Spring Data — query projections**
- DTO projections via `SELECT new com.example.UserSummary(u.id, u.name) ...`
- Interface-based projections also work

**Records in Maps and Sets**
- Work perfectly — `equals`/`hashCode` based on all components
- Useful as composite keys

**Style recommendations**
- DTOs, value objects, return-grouping, events: records
- Entities, services, mutable state, identity: classes
- Compact constructor for validation
- Defensive copy collection components
- Don't add many custom methods to records — if you need behavior, consider a class
- Single-component records are sometimes overkill — use the underlying type

**Recommendation:** Use **records** as your default for any **immutable data carrier** — DTOs, value objects, domain events, method return types that need to group multiple values. The 1-line declaration replaces 20+ lines of class boilerplate. Use a **compact constructor** for **validation and normalization** — fail fast on invalid input, normalize values (uppercase, strip whitespace, defensive copy collections). Pair records with **sealed interfaces** (Java 17) for **ADT-style domain modeling** — each variant is a record, the sealed type is the closed hierarchy, and **pattern matching switch** (Java 21) gives you compile-time exhaustive matching with deconstruction. Don't use records for **JPA entities** (need mutable state and no-arg constructor), **identity-based objects** (auto-generated equals is wrong for ID-based identity), or **mutable state**. Don't try to extend classes — records can only implement interfaces. Records win over **Lombok `@Value`** for new code: native to the JDK, no annotation processor, recognized by all tools, and they deconstruct in pattern matching. Lombok still has its place for `@Builder` and mutable `@Data` — they're not in competition for the same feature. The mental model: **records are a class shorthand for immutable data with value semantics** — nothing more, nothing less. They pair beautifully with sealed types, pattern matching, and the modern Java functional style.

sections.title: The Problem Sealed Types Solve
sections.content:
Java has long had two extremes for class extensibility:
- **`final`** — nothing can extend.
- **Open** (default) — anything can extend.

But sometimes you want a **middle ground**: a type that can be extended, but only by a **specific, known set** of subtypes. Examples:
- A `Shape` that should only be `Circle`, `Square`, or `Triangle`.
- A `PaymentMethod` that should only be `CreditCard`, `BankTransfer`, `CryptoPayment`, `Wallet`.
- A `Result<T>` that's either `Success<T>` or `Failure<T>`.
- An AST node that's one of a fixed set of expression types.

With pre-Java-17 tools, you had to:
- Use a regular interface and hope no one adds rogue implementations.
- Use package-private constructors as a hack.
- Use enums (limited to constants, can't carry data well).

Sealed types (Java 17, JEP 409) make this **first-class**:
```java
public sealed class Shape
    permits Circle, Square, Triangle {}

public final class Circle   extends Shape {}
public final class Square   extends Shape {}
public final class Triangle extends Shape {}
```

Now `Shape` is **closed** — the compiler enforces that only those three classes can extend it. Combined with **pattern matching switch** (Java 21), this enables **exhaustive type matching** with compile-time verification.

sections.title: Syntax — `sealed`, `permits`, `final`, `sealed`, `non-sealed`
sections.content:
**Basic sealed declaration**:
```java
public sealed interface Shape
    permits Circle, Square, Triangle {}
```

**The `permits` clause**:
- Lists every class that may **directly** extend the sealed type.
- All listed types must be in the same module (or same package for unnamed modules).
- Order doesn't matter.
- Can be omitted **only if** all permitted subtypes are in the same compilation unit (single file).

**Each permitted subtype must declare its own modifier**:
```java
public final   class Circle   implements Shape {}  // closes the hierarchy here
public sealed  class Square   implements Shape    // continues sealed
    permits SquareUnit, SquareLarge {}
public non-sealed class Triangle implements Shape {} // opens back up
```

**Three modifiers for permitted subtypes**:
- **`final`** — cannot be extended further (most common).
- **`sealed`** — continues the closed hierarchy with its own `permits`.
- **`non-sealed`** — opens this branch back up to arbitrary extension.

**Records are implicitly `final`** — perfect with sealed:
```java
public sealed interface Shape
    permits Circle, Square, Triangle {}

public record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {}
public record Square(double side) implements Shape {}
public record Triangle(double base, double height) implements Shape {}
```
Most real-world sealed hierarchies use records as the leaves.

**Same-file shorthand** — omit `permits` if all subtypes are in the same file:
```java
public sealed interface Result<T> {
    record Success<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {}
    record Failure<T>(String error) implements Result<T> {}
    // No `permits` needed because all impls are nested in the same file
}
```

sections.title: Exhaustive Pattern Matching — The Big Win
Real-World Domain Modeling
Restrictions and Module/Package Rules
sections.content:
**Same module / package requirement**:
- All permitted subtypes must be in the **same module** as the sealed type.
- For unnamed modules (no `module-info.java`), they must be in the **same package**.
- This ensures the compiler can verify the closed hierarchy at compile time.

**No external extension**:
- A user of your library cannot add subtypes to your sealed hierarchy.
- This is the whole point — it's truly closed.
- For extensible domains (plugins, third-party impls), use a regular interface.

**Permitted subtypes must be accessible**:
- All permits-listed types must be visible to the sealed type at compile time.
- Public sealed type with package-private subtypes works only within the package.

**No cycles**:
- A sealed type can't have itself in its permits list (silly to mention but compiler enforces).

**Reflection access**:
- `Class.getPermittedSubclasses()` returns the array of permitted subtypes.
- `Class.isSealed()` returns true for sealed types.
- Useful for frameworks doing introspection.

**Bytecode**:
- The `permits` clause is stored in the class file as the **PermittedSubclasses attribute**.
- The JVM enforces the restriction at class load time — attempting to load a class that extends a sealed type without permission throws a `IncompatibleClassChangeError`.

**Generic sealed types**:
```java
public sealed interface Tree<T> permits Leaf, Branch {}
public record Leaf<T>(T value)                   implements Tree<T> {}
public record Branch<T>(Tree<T> left, Tree<T> right) implements Tree<T> {}
```

**Inheritance with sealed**:
```java
public sealed class Animal permits Mammal, Bird, Fish {}
public sealed class Mammal extends Animal permits Dog, Cat {}
public final class Dog extends Mammal {}
public final class Cat extends Mammal {}
public non-sealed class Bird extends Animal {}  // anyone can extend Bird
public final class Fish extends Animal {}
```
This lets you have a closed top-level hierarchy with mixed sealed/open branches.

sections.title: When to Use vs Not Use Sealed Types
sections.content:
**Use sealed types for**:
- **Closed business domains** — payment methods, event types, command/result types.
- **AST nodes** for interpreters/compilers/parsers.
- **State machines** — each state is a permitted subtype.
- **Result/Option/Either** types for functional error handling.
- **Anywhere you'd use a Scala sealed trait or Kotlin sealed class**.
- **Combined with records for pure data ADTs**.

**Don't use sealed types for**:
- **Open extension points** (plugins, library extension hooks) — use a regular interface.
- **Single-implementation types** — just use `final` or no modifier.
- **JPA entity hierarchies** with TABLE_PER_CLASS or JOINED inheritance — sealed adds rigidity that may conflict with persistence flexibility.
- **Cases with only 2–3 known subtypes that never change** — sealed is fine but a regular `final` hierarchy works too if no exhaustiveness check is needed.

**Sealed vs `final`**:
- `final` = nothing extends.
- `sealed` = a known set extends, and only that set.
- Use `sealed` when you want polymorphism over a closed set.

**Sealed vs interface (open)**:
- Open interface = any class anywhere can implement.
- Sealed = compiler-enforced closed set.
- Use sealed when the closed set is intentional.

**Sealed vs enum**:
- Enum = fixed set of constants (no per-instance data, no per-instance behavior beyond methods).
- Sealed = fixed set of subtypes (each can carry different data, have different methods).
- Use sealed when each variant carries distinct data; use enum for flag-like constants.

**Best practices**:
- **Combine with records** for pure data variants.
- **Use exhaustive switch expressions** — don't add `default` (loses the maintenance benefit).
- **Single-file shorthand**: omit `permits` if all subtypes are nested in the same file.
- **Use `non-sealed`** sparingly — it opens up the hierarchy and breaks exhaustiveness.
- **Keep the hierarchy shallow** — deeply nested sealed types get hard to reason about.
- **Document the rationale** — future maintainers need to know why this is sealed.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Sealed classes (Java 17, JEP 409) let you explicitly restrict which classes can extend or implement them. Instead of any class anywhere being free to extend your base type, you declare the closed set with `permits`.

**Syntax**
- `public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Triangle {}`
- Each permitted subtype must declare `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`
- All permitted subtypes must be in the same module (or same package for unnamed modules)
- Same-file shorthand: omit `permits` if all subtypes are nested

**Three modifiers for permitted subtypes**
- **`final`** — closes the hierarchy here (most common)
- **`sealed`** — continues with its own permits list
- **`non-sealed`** — opens this branch back up to arbitrary extension

**Records are implicitly `final`** — perfect leaves
- `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square` + `record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}`
- Most real-world sealed hierarchies use records as leaves

**The big payoff: exhaustive pattern matching (Java 21)**
- Switch over a sealed type with no `default` needed
- Compiler verifies all permitted subtypes are covered
- Adding a new subtype → compile error in every switch in the codebase
- Maintenance superpower for evolving domain models

**With record deconstruction (JEP 440)**
- `case Circle(double r) -> Math.PI * r * r`
- Destructure inline in the case

**With `when` guards**
- `case Circle c when c.radius() > 100 -> "big circle"`

**Sealed + records + pattern switch = ADTs in Java**
- Same expressive power as Scala case classes or Rust enums
- Compile-time type safety, no nulls, exhaustive matching

**Real-world domain modeling**

**Result type for functional error handling**
- `sealed interface Result<T> permits Success, Failure`
- `record Success<T>(T value)` and `record Failure<T>(String error)`
- Pattern match for safe handling

**Payment methods**
- `sealed interface PaymentMethod permits CreditCard, BankTransfer, Wallet, Crypto`
- Adding ApplePay forces every processor to handle it

**Domain events**
- `sealed interface OrderEvent permits Placed, Confirmed, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled`

**AST nodes for interpreters**
- `sealed interface Expr permits Lit, Var, Add, Mul, Let`
- Recursive evaluator via pattern match

**Module/package rules**
- Permitted subtypes must be in the same module (or package for unnamed modules)
- Compiler must see them at compile time
- JVM enforces via PermittedSubclasses attribute in class file
- Loading an unauthorized extension throws IncompatibleClassChangeError

**No external extension**
- Library users cannot add subtypes to your sealed hierarchy
- This is the whole point — it's truly closed
- For extensible domains (plugins), use regular interfaces

**Reflection support**
- `Class.getPermittedSubclasses()` returns the array
- `Class.isSealed()` returns true
- Useful for frameworks doing introspection

**Sealed vs final**
- `final` — nothing extends
- `sealed` — a known set extends
- Use sealed when you want polymorphism over a closed set

**Sealed vs open interface**
- Open — anyone can implement
- Sealed — compiler-enforced closed set
- Use sealed when the closed set is intentional

**Sealed vs enum**
- Enum — fixed set of constants (limited per-instance data)
- Sealed — fixed set of subtypes, each can carry distinct data and have distinct methods
- Use sealed when variants carry different shapes of data

**When to use sealed types**
- Closed business domains (payment methods, event types, command/result)
- AST nodes
- State machines (each state as permitted subtype)
- Result/Option/Either functional types
- Anywhere you'd use Scala sealed trait or Kotlin sealed class
- Combine with records for pure data ADTs

**When NOT to use sealed types**
- Open extension points (plugins, library hooks) — use regular interfaces
- Single-implementation types — just use `final`
- JPA entity hierarchies (sealed conflicts with persistence flexibility)
- Cases without exhaustive switch needs (sealed adds ceremony for no benefit)

**Best practices**
- Combine with records for pure data variants
- Use exhaustive switch expressions — don't add `default` (defeats the maintenance benefit)
- Same-file shorthand for small hierarchies
- Use `non-sealed` sparingly (it opens up the branch)
- Keep the hierarchy shallow
- Document why it's sealed

**Replaces Visitor pattern for most uses**
- One switch method instead of separate visitor class per operation
- New variants added in one place
- Compile-time exhaustiveness for free
- Visitor still useful when you can't modify the data classes

**Recommendation:** Use **sealed classes/interfaces** whenever you have a **closed business domain** with a known, finite set of variants — payment methods, event types, command/result types, AST nodes, state machines. Combine with **records** for pure data variants and **pattern matching switch** (Java 21) for **exhaustive type dispatch with no `default` needed**. The key win is the **maintenance superpower**: adding a new permitted subtype forces every switch in the codebase to be updated (compile error), so you can't silently miss a case. This is what functional languages (Scala, Kotlin, Rust, Haskell) have had for years — Java now has it too. For **truly extensible** types (plugins, library extension hooks), keep using a **regular interface** — sealed is for closed sets. For **single-implementation** types, just use `final`. For **enum-like** flags with no per-instance data, use an `enum`. Reach for sealed when each variant carries **different data shapes** and you need **type-safe exhaustive dispatch**. Use **`non-sealed`** sparingly — it opens up a branch and breaks the exhaustiveness guarantee. Don't add **`default`** to switches over sealed types — it defeats the compile-time check that's the whole point. Sealed + records + pattern matching is the Java answer to ADTs, and it's one of the most powerful additions to the language in years.

questions.question: What are Helpful NullPointerExceptions in Java 14+? How do they improve debugging vs the old generic message?
questions.title: Helpful NullPointerExceptions (Java 14+) — Tell Me Which Variable Was Null
questions.direct_answer: **Helpful NullPointerExceptions** (Java 14, JEP 358; on by default since Java 15) replace the old useless `NullPointerException` message — just `NullPointerException` with a stack frame — with a **precise message that names the exact variable or expression that was null**. For `a.b().c().d()` where `c()` returns null, the old NPE just told you the line; the new NPE says: **`Cannot invoke "X.d()" because the return value of "Y.c()" is null`**. The JVM analyzes the bytecode at the throw site to reconstruct the source-level expression that produced the null. This eliminates the entire class of "NPE on line 42 of a long chain" debugging sessions — you immediately know which sub-expression failed. The feature is **enabled by default since Java 15** (`-XX:+ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages` is on); you can disable with `-XX:-ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages` (very rarely useful). Performance impact: the message is **only constructed lazily** when `getMessage()` is called — zero cost for thrown-and-discarded NPEs in tight loops. Limitations: requires the bytecode to be present (works for compiled classes; may not work for some lambda call sites or proxies); requires line/source info to be useful (compile with `-g`). It works for **field access**, **method invocation**, **array access**, **assignment**, and **unboxing** — covering essentially all the common null-dereference paths. The takeaway for interviews: this is one of the highest-ROI JVM improvements in years, removing noise from debugging at zero cost.

sections.title: The Old NPE — A Debugging Nightmare
The New NPE — Tell Me Exactly What Was Null
How It Works
sections.content:
When an NPE is about to be thrown, the JVM:

1. **Looks at the bytecode** at the throw site.
2. **Identifies the dereferenced expression** (a `getfield`, `invokevirtual`, `aaload`, etc.).
3. **Reconstructs the source-level expression** by walking the bytecode and class file metadata.
4. **Constructs the message** including which sub-expression was null and what operation was attempted.

**Lazy construction**:
- The message is **NOT** computed when the NPE is thrown.
- It's computed only when `getMessage()` (or `toString()`) is called.
- For NPEs that are caught and ignored (e.g., in tight loops), the cost is zero.
- The message is cached after first construction.

**JVM flag**:
- **`-XX:+ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages`** — enable (default in Java 15+).
- **`-XX:-ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages`** — disable (rarely useful; perhaps for security-sensitive code where you don't want stack details in error messages).

**Limitations**:
- Requires the bytecode to be available at runtime — works for normal compiled classes; may not work for some dynamically generated proxies, lambdas in some configurations, or stripped class files.
- The message reconstruction is **best-effort** — in obscure bytecode patterns, the message may be less precise.
- For **stack trace line numbers** to be useful, compile with `-g` (default for Maven/Gradle).
- Not all NPE messages benefit equally; complex generated bytecode may produce less helpful messages.

sections.title: Real-World Impact
sections.content:
**Production debugging — before**:
```
NullPointerException at OrderProcessor.process(OrderProcessor.java:127)
```
Developer:
1. Open the file at line 127.
2. See `order.getCustomer().getAccount().getBalance().getAmount();`.
3. Add logging for each subexpression.
4. Redeploy.
5. Wait for the NPE to recur.
6. Repeat if logging isn't quite right.

Total: hours to days of debugging cycle.

**Production debugging — after**:
```
NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "BigDecimal.getAmount()" because the
  return value of "Account.getBalance()" is null
  at OrderProcessor.process(OrderProcessor.java:127)
```
Developer:
1. Read message: `Account.getBalance()` returned null.
2. Look at why — customer's account has no balance set; data import bug.
3. Fix at the source.

Total: minutes.

**The cost savings across an organization** are substantial. NPEs are the most common Java exception in production; trimming each debugging session from hours to minutes pays for the entire JEP many times over.

**Logging integration**:
```java
try {
    process(order);
} catch (NullPointerException npe) {
    log.error("Failed to process order: {}", order.getId(), npe);
    // The full helpful message is in the npe.getMessage()
}
```
Log aggregators (Splunk, Datadog, ELK) immediately surface the precise null source.

sections.title: When (Not) to Disable, Best Practices
sections.content:
**When to disable** (`-XX:-ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages`):
- **Almost never**.
- Security-sensitive code where you don't want stack details in user-facing messages — but you should already be sanitizing exception messages, not relying on the JVM to omit details.
- Some legacy frameworks may have parsed the old generic NPE message; very rare and easily fixed.

**Performance considerations**:
- **Zero cost** for thrown-and-discarded NPEs (lazy message).
- **Tiny cost** for NPEs whose message is read — bytecode walk is O(1) per throw.
- **Caching** — message computed once per NPE instance.
- For high-throughput code that throws+catches NPEs intentionally (an anti-pattern, but exists): no perf hit.

**Best practices**:
- **Always run on Java 15+** — you get this feature for free.
- **Never catch NPE** to ignore it — the helpful message is wasted; instead, fix the null source.
- **Use Optional or @Nullable annotations** at API boundaries to make null-ness explicit.
- **Log NPE messages** as part of your error tracking — the helpful text is gold.
- **Combine with pattern matching** for null safety: Java 21's `case null -> ...` in switch.
- **Consider null-safe APIs** in new code (Optional return types, Objects.requireNonNull on entry).

**Other Java 14+ features in the same spirit** — reduce debugging overhead:
- **Better deprecation warnings** with `since` and `forRemoval`.
- **Improved stack traces** for `String.valueOf` failures.
- **Records and sealed types** make impossible states impossible — fewer NPEs at all.

**Migration checklist**:
- Verify Java 15+ is in production.
- Confirm `-XX:+ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages` is on (it's default; should be).
- Update CI/test logs to capture the new richer messages.
- Train developers to read and trust the new messages.

**Unboxing**
- `Cannot invoke "Integer.intValue()" because the return value of "Map.get(Object)" is null`
- This is the classic 'unboxing null Integer' bug

**Limitations**
- Bytecode must be present — works for normal compiled classes
- May not work for some dynamically generated proxies or lambda call sites
- Best-effort — obscure bytecode may produce less precise messages
- Line numbers need `-g` (default for Maven/Gradle)

**Real-world impact**

**Before**: NPE on line 127 → add logging → redeploy → wait for recurrence → repeat. Hours to days of debugging cycle.

**After**: read the message, see which method returned null, fix at source. Minutes.

Massive cost savings across an organization. NPEs are the most common Java exception in production.

**Best practices**
- Always run Java 15+ — you get this for free
- Never catch NPE to ignore it — the helpful message is wasted; fix the null source
- Use Optional or @Nullable annotations at API boundaries
- Log NPE messages — the helpful text is gold for error tracking
- Combine with Java 21 `case null -> ...` in switch for explicit null handling
- Consider null-safe APIs in new code: Optional returns, Objects.requireNonNull on entry

**When to disable**
- Almost never
- Security-sensitive code where stack details shouldn't appear in user-facing messages — but you should sanitize exception messages anyway, not rely on JVM omission
- Some legacy frameworks parsing the old generic NPE message — very rare

**Combines with other features**
- Records and sealed types reduce null-ness in domain models
- Optional makes absence explicit at API boundaries
- Pattern matching with `case null` (Java 21) explicit null cases
- Bean Validation @NotNull on fields

**Recommendation:** Just **make sure you're on Java 15+** and **don't disable it**. The feature is **on by default**, has **zero performance cost** when messages aren't read (lazy construction), and produces **massive debugging time savings** in production. The new NPE message names the exact sub-expression that was null — turning multi-hour debugging cycles into minutes. **Never catch NPE to ignore it** — the helpful message is wasted, and you're hiding a bug. **Log NPE messages** as part of your error tracking; the precise text is gold for correlating issues. **Combine with Optional**, **sealed types** (impossible states impossible), **records** (immutable defaults), and **pattern matching with `case null`** (Java 21) for end-to-end null safety — helpful NPEs are the safety net for when null does sneak through. The JVM flag **`-XX:+ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages`** is the canonical name; almost no one needs to think about it because it's the default. This is one of the **highest-ROI JVM improvements in years**: zero cost, massive benefit, just upgrade your runtime.
